rules: Helpful free tips for heating and air, plumbing and electrical shop owners. Give, don't sell (Hormozi give until they ask). No prices, no rank or job promises, no phone numbers. Image card per post at sites/getbookedoutsolutions.com/img/social/tip-NN.png (https://getbookedoutsolutions.com/img/social/tip-NN.png).

posts.headline: The quote you already gave is your cheapest lead
posts.x:
The cheapest job you'll book this month is probably sitting in your sent folder.

Most homeowners who don't answer a quote aren't saying no. They got busy.

A short note 2 days later, another at day 7, and a last one at day 14 brings a lot of them back.
posts.long:
The cheapest job you'll book this month is probably sitting in your sent folder.

Most homeowners who don't answer a quote aren't saying no. They got busy, the kids got sick, they meant to call you back.

A simple follow-up rhythm that works:
Day 2: "Just checking you got the quote. Any questions?"
Day 7: Answer the question they're most likely stuck on (price, timing, financing).
Day 14: "Should I keep this open for you, or close it out?"

That last one gets more replies than you'd think. People like being given an easy way to answer.

posts.headline: Answer every review, even the 5-star ones
posts.x:
Answer every Google review, even the 5-star ones.

The next customer reads your replies to see how you treat people. A quick thank-you with the job and the town in it ("Glad the new water heater is keeping up, Tom") shows you're real.
posts.long:
Answer every Google review, even the 5-star ones.

You're not really writing to the person who left it. You're writing to the next homeowner scrolling your profile at 9 pm deciding who to call.

Keep it short and specific: thank them by name, mention the job and the town if they did ("Glad the new water heater is keeping up, Tom"), and sign it with your name.

Three lines, about a minute each. Do it the same week the review comes in.

posts.headline: How to answer a bad review
posts.x:
How to answer a bad review without making it worse:

1. Thank them for telling you.
2. One sentence on what you'll do.
3. Take it offline: "Call me directly at the shop."

No arguing, no job details, no blaming. You're writing for the next customer, not to win.
posts.long:
A 1-star review feels personal. Here's how I'd answer one without making it worse:

1. Thank them for telling you. It sounds backwards, but it calms everyone down.
2. One sentence on what you'll do about it.
3. Take it offline: "Please call me directly at the shop so I can make this right."

What to leave out: arguing, job details, blaming the customer or the tech.

The homeowner reading it later doesn't care who was right. They care whether you handle problems like an adult.

posts.headline: 5 things to check on your Google profile today
posts.x:
5 things to check on your Google Business Profile today:

- Hours match when someone actually picks up
- Service area lists the towns you want work in
- Main category is your real money job
- Photos from the last 30 days
- Phone number rings a person, not a dead line
posts.long:
5 things to check on your Google Business Profile today (10 minutes):

1. Hours match when someone actually picks up the phone.
2. Service area lists the towns you want more work in, not just your home town.
3. Your main category is your real money job.
4. You have photos from the last 30 days. Real jobs, your truck, your crew.
5. The phone number rings a person, not a dead line or a full voicemail.

Google shows the profiles that look active and accurate. These five are free to fix.

posts.headline: Ask for the review while you're still in the driveway
posts.x:
The best time to ask for a Google review is while the customer is still smiling.

Before you pull out of the driveway: "Would you mind leaving us a quick review? I'll text you the link." Then send it right then, not tomorrow.
posts.long:
The best time to ask for a Google review is while the customer is still standing there happy.

Before you pull out of the driveway: "If you were happy with today, would you mind leaving us a quick review? I'll text you the link right now."

Then actually send it right then. Tomorrow the moment is gone.

Ask everyone the same way. Don't pick only the happy-looking ones and never offer anything in return; Google doesn't allow it, and it isn't needed.

posts.headline: Slow season is for old customers
posts.x:
Slow season? Before you spend a dollar on ads, email the customers you already have.

They know you, they trust you, and many are due for a tune-up, a flush or a check. One friendly note to past customers often fills more of the calendar than a new ad.
posts.long:
Slow season? Before you spend a dollar on ads, reach out to the customers you already have.

They know you and trust you, and a lot of them are due: tune-ups, water heater flushes, panel checks, filter changes.

One short, friendly note works better than a sales pitch:
"Hi Linda, it's been about a year since we serviced your system. Want me to put you on the schedule before it gets busy?"

Your customer list is the most valuable list you own. Use it before you rent someone else's.

posts.headline: A missed call is a missed job
posts.x:
Most people who call a home service company and get voicemail don't leave a message. They call the next shop on the list.

If you can't pick up, text back within 5 minutes: "Sorry we missed you, how can we help?" It saves more jobs than you'd think.
posts.long:
Most people who call a home service company and get voicemail don't leave a message. They just call the next shop on Google.

If you can't pick up (you're under a sink or in an attic, I get it), the next best thing is a quick text back within 5 minutes:

"Sorry we missed your call. This is Mike at Smith Heating. How can we help?"

Most phones and business lines can do this automatically. Set it up once and it works every day.

posts.headline: What I learned running a dry cleaner
posts.x:
I ran a dry cleaner in Santee, CA for 6 years. The biggest lesson: customers don't pick the shop with the best work. They pick the one that answers, follows up and makes it easy.

Same thing is true for HVAC, plumbing and electrical.
posts.long:
Before Booked Out, I ran a dry cleaner in Santee, California for about 6 years.

The biggest thing I learned: customers mostly can't tell who does the best work. They pick the shop that answers the phone, gets back to them, and makes it easy.

We answered everyone. Every call, every complaint, every review. That's what grew the business.

It's the same for heating and air, plumbing and electrical. Your work might be the best in town, but the shop that answers and follows up gets the call.

posts.headline: Put the price range on the quote follow-up
posts.x:
Homeowners often go quiet on a quote because they're scared of the number, not because they found someone cheaper.

In your follow-up, mention options: "If the full replacement is more than you planned, we can talk about a repair first or a payment plan."
posts.long:
Homeowners often go quiet on a quote because the number scared them, not because they found someone cheaper.

So in your follow-up, give them a way to keep talking:
"If the full replacement is more than you planned for, I'm happy to walk through a repair option first, or a payment plan if you offer one."

You're not lowering your price. You're giving them a reason to call you back instead of disappearing.

posts.headline: Your website needs one thing above the fold
posts.x:
Your website needs one thing at the top that a homeowner can see in 3 seconds on a phone: what you do, the towns you serve, and a big button to call or ask for a quote.

Everything else can go further down.
posts.long:
Pull up your website on your phone right now. In 3 seconds, can a stranger tell:

- What you do (heating and air, plumbing, electrical)
- What towns you serve
- How to reach you (a big call button and a quote form)

If not, that's the first fix. Most people looking for a contractor are on their phone, in a hurry, with a problem. Make the next step obvious and put everything else further down the page.

posts.headline: Text before the tech shows up
posts.x:
Nobody likes opening the door to a stranger.

A quick text before the tech leaves for the job fixes that: "Hi, this is Marcus from ___. I'm on my way, about 25 minutes out." Add his photo if your system allows it.

The homeowner knows who's coming. Fewer no-answers at the door.
posts.long:
Nobody likes opening the door to a stranger.

A short text before the tech heads out fixes most of that:
"Hi, this is Marcus from ___. I'm on my way, about 25 minutes out."

Add a photo of the tech if your software allows it. Now the homeowner knows who's coming, has time to put the dog up, and is home when the truck pulls in.

It costs nothing, and it's the first thing people mention when they say a company was easy to work with.

posts.headline: Real photos beat stock photos
posts.x:
Homeowners can spot a stock photo from across the room.

On your Google profile and website, use real ones: your trucks, your shop, your techs in uniform, a finished install.

Phone photos are fine. Real is what people trust.
posts.long:
Homeowners can spot a stock photo from across the room.

On your Google profile and your website, swap them for real ones:
- Your trucks, clean, with the logo showing
- Your shop or warehouse
- Your techs in uniform (with their OK)
- A finished install or a clean panel

Phone photos are fine. Good light and a clean background matter more than the camera.

When someone is picking between three companies they've never heard of, real faces and real trucks are what make you feel like a real business.

posts.headline: List every town you actually serve
posts.x:
If you serve 12 towns but your website only names one, Google has to guess.

List each town you really work in, on your service area page and in your Google profile's service areas.

Only the towns you'll actually drive to.
posts.long:
If you work in 12 towns but your website only names one, Google has to guess where you go.

Two quick fixes:
1. In your Google Business Profile, set your service areas to the towns you really serve.
2. On your website, have a service area page that names each town, with a line or two about the work you do there.

Keep it honest. Only list the places you'll actually drive to on a Tuesday afternoon. A homeowner 50 minutes out who calls and gets told no is a wasted call for both of you.

posts.headline: The first 10 seconds of the phone call
posts.x:
How you answer sets the whole call.

Say the company name, your name, and a question: "Thanks for calling ___, this is Sarah. What's going on at the house?"

Then let them talk. People calling a trade usually have a problem they want to explain.
posts.long:
How your phone gets answered sets the tone for the whole job.

A simple opener that works:
"Thanks for calling ___, this is Sarah. What's going on at the house?"

Then stop and let them talk. Most people calling a plumber or an electrician are stressed and want to explain the problem. Letting them get it out builds trust faster than anything you could say.

Write the opener on a sticky note by every phone in the office. Whoever picks up should sound the same.

posts.headline: Maintenance plans carry you through the slow months
posts.x:
The shops that stay steady in slow months usually have one thing in common: customers on a maintenance plan.

Two visits a year, scheduled ahead, filling the calendar when the phone goes quiet.

Ask every repair customer if they'd like one.
posts.long:
The shops that stay steady in slow months usually have something in common: a list of customers on a maintenance plan.

Two visits a year, booked ahead. Those visits fill the calendar when the phone goes quiet, and they find the repairs before they turn into emergencies.

The easiest time to offer one is right after a repair, while the homeowner is glad it's fixed:
"Want us to put you on the schedule to check it twice a year so this doesn't happen again?"

You don't need a fancy program to start. A spreadsheet and a reminder works.

posts.headline: Give homeowners a checklist they'll keep
posts.x:
Want homeowners to remember your name? Give them something useful.

A one-page "before winter" checklist with your logo: change the filter, check the smoke detectors, find your water shutoff.

They'll keep it on the fridge.
posts.long:
Want homeowners to remember your name next time something breaks? Give them something useful now.

A simple one-page seasonal checklist with your logo and number on it:
- Change the furnace filter
- Test smoke and CO detectors
- Know where the main water shutoff is
- Disconnect garden hoses before a freeze

Leave it at every job, email it to past customers, post it on your Google profile.

It's not an ad. It's help. And it ends up on the fridge, which is where you want your name.

posts.headline: What your after-hours voicemail should say
posts.x:
A voicemail that just says "leave a message" loses people.

Tell callers when they'll hear back: "We're closed now. Leave your name and number, and we'll call you back by 8 tomorrow morning."

A clear time keeps them from calling the next company.
posts.long:
A voicemail that just says "leave a message" loses people. They hang up and call the next name on the list.

Tell callers exactly what happens next:
"Thanks for calling ___. We're closed right now. Leave your name, number and what's going on, and we'll call you back by 8 tomorrow morning."

If you take emergency calls, say how to reach you. If you don't, say that too, kindly.

Then keep the promise. Calling back at 8:00 sharp is how a voicemail turns into a booked job.

posts.headline: Answer web forms fast
posts.x:
A homeowner who fills out your website form is usually filling out two or three others.

The company that gets back to them first often gets the job.

Set your phone to alert you on every form, and reply within minutes, not hours.
posts.long:
A homeowner who fills out the form on your website is usually filling out two or three others at the same time.

The company that gets back to them first often wins, simply because they answered while the problem was still top of mind.

Make it easy on yourself:
- Have form messages go to your phone, not just an inbox nobody checks
- Keep a short reply ready to send: "Got your message about the water heater. I can call you in 10 minutes, does that work?"
- Call, don't just email

Minutes, not hours.

posts.headline: Put the tech's name in the review request
posts.x:
"Leave us a review" is easy to ignore.

"Would you mind sharing how Jake did today?" is not.

People like helping a person more than helping a company. Use the tech's name every time you ask.
posts.long:
"Please leave us a review" is easy to ignore.

"Would you mind sharing how Jake did today?" is a lot harder to ignore.

People would rather help a person than a company. When the review request names the tech who was in their house, it feels personal, and the reviews you get mention your techs by name. That helps the next homeowner too, because they can see real people doing the work.

Send it the same day, with the direct link, so it takes them one tap.

posts.headline: Post a job photo every week
posts.x:
Your Google profile isn't a sign you hang once. It works better when it looks alive.

Once a week, post a photo from a real job with a line about it: "New water heater in Smyrna today."

Ten minutes a week.
posts.long:
Your Google Business Profile isn't a sign you hang once and forget. It works better when it looks alive.

Once a week, add a post with a photo from a real job and one line about it:
"Swapped out a 15-year-old water heater in Smyrna this morning."

No customer names, no house numbers. Just the work and the town.

It shows homeowners you're busy and active, and it shows them the kind of work you actually do. Ten minutes a week, and it adds up.

posts.headline: Before and after photos, done right
posts.x:
Before and after photos are some of the best things you can post.

Two rules: ask the homeowner first, and keep house numbers, faces and street signs out of the shot.

A crusty old panel next to a clean new one tells the story.
posts.long:
Before and after photos are some of the most convincing things a trade company can post.

Do them right:
- Ask the homeowner if it's OK first
- Keep house numbers, faces, family photos and street signs out of the frame
- Shoot both from the same angle

A corroded old water heater next to the clean new install. A messy panel next to a neat one. Nobody needs a paragraph to get it.

Tell your techs to take the "before" shot before they touch anything. That's the one people forget.

posts.headline: Give options on every quote
posts.x:
A single price is a yes-or-no question. Most people say no.

Give two or three options: the repair, the repair plus the part that's about to go, and the replacement.

Now they're choosing which, not whether.
posts.long:
A quote with one price is a yes-or-no question, and a lot of people say no.

Try giving two or three options instead:
1. Fix what's broken today
2. Fix it and replace the part that's close to failing
3. Replace the whole unit, with the longer warranty

Now the homeowner is choosing which option fits them, not whether to hire you. Many will pick the middle one.

Be honest about each option. The goal isn't to push the biggest one. It's to let people decide with the full picture.

posts.headline: Write the quote in plain words
posts.x:
"Replaced 40/5 MFD capacitor" means nothing to most homeowners.

"Replaced the part that helps your AC start up. It had worn out." means everything.

Plain words on the quote get more yeses.
posts.long:
"Replace 40/5 MFD dual run capacitor" means nothing to most homeowners.

"Replace the part that helps your AC start up. It's worn out, which is why the unit kept shutting off." means a lot.

Keep the part numbers for your records. On the quote the homeowner reads, write:
- What's wrong, in plain words
- What happens if they wait
- What you'll do

People don't say yes to things they don't understand. Plain words take the fear out of the price.

posts.headline: When they say "we'll think about it"
posts.x:
"We'll think about it" usually means there's one thing they're stuck on.

Ask kindly: "Totally fair. Is it the price, the timing, or something about the work?"

Then answer that one thing.
posts.long:
"We'll think about it" almost never means they want to sit and think. It usually means there's one thing bothering them that they haven't said.

Ask, kindly and without pressure:
"Totally fair. Just so I can help, is it the price, the timing, or something about the work itself?"

Most people will tell you. Then you can answer that one thing: show a cheaper option, offer a different day, or explain the part they were unsure about.

If they still want to wait, that's fine. Follow up in a couple of days.

posts.headline: Old quotes are worth a winter check-in
posts.x:
Look back at quotes from this past year that never turned into jobs.

A short, friendly note now: "Hi, just checking in on the furnace we looked at in the spring. Still running OK?"

Some of those are ready now.
posts.long:
Every shop has a pile of quotes from the past year that never turned into jobs. The homeowner wasn't ready, money was tight, or they just forgot.

Some of them are ready now.

Send a short, friendly check-in:
"Hi, this is ___. We looked at your furnace back in the spring. Just checking in to see how it's running now that it's cold."

No pressure, no discount, just a real question. The ones whose unit is struggling will answer. It's the easiest work you'll book all month.

posts.headline: Ask every caller how they found you
posts.x:
If you don't know where your calls come from, you can't tell what's working.

One question on every call: "How did you hear about us?"

Write it down. In a month you'll know where to spend your time.
posts.long:
If you don't know where your calls come from, you can't tell what's working and what's wasting money.

The simplest tracking there is: ask every new caller "How did you hear about us?" and write the answer down. Google, a neighbor, the truck, a past customer, Facebook.

Keep a tally for a month. You'll probably be surprised. Most owners find that one or two sources bring in most of the good jobs.

Then you know where to put more effort, and what to stop paying for.

posts.headline: Make friends with the other trades
posts.x:
The plumber sees the old electrical panel. The electrician sees the leaking water heater. The HVAC tech sees both.

Get to know one good shop in each trade you don't do, and send each other the work you can't take.
posts.long:
A plumber sees the scary old electrical panel. An electrician sees the leaking water heater. An HVAC tech sees both.

Every trade runs into work it doesn't do. Get to know one good, honest shop in each trade you don't cover, and pass along the jobs you can't take.

The homeowner gets someone you trust instead of a random search result. You look like the company that knows people. And the other shop remembers who sent them that job.

Coffee with another owner is time well spent.

posts.headline: Realtors and property managers call again and again
posts.x:
One homeowner calls you once or twice a year. A property manager might call every week.

Realtors need inspections fixed fast before closing. Property managers need someone reliable for their rentals.

Be the one who shows up on time.
posts.long:
A homeowner might call you once or twice a year. A property manager with 40 rentals might call every week. A realtor with a closing on Friday needs inspection repairs done now.

These are some of the best repeat customers a trade shop can have. What they care about:
- Showing up when you said you would
- Clear photos and notes of what you did
- An invoice that's easy to forward

Introduce yourself to a few local property managers and realtors. Then be the most reliable call on their list.

posts.headline: A thank-you note after a big job
posts.x:
After a big install, mail a handwritten thank-you card.

Two lines, signed by the tech or the owner.

Almost nobody does this anymore, so people remember the ones who do.
posts.long:
After a big job, a new system, a repipe, a panel upgrade, mail a handwritten thank-you card.

Two or three lines is enough:
"Thanks for trusting us with your new AC. It was great working with you. If anything doesn't feel right, call me directly."

Signed by the tech or the owner.

Hardly anyone does this anymore, so the people who get one remember it. It's the card that ends up on the fridge, and the name they give their neighbor.

posts.headline: Read your bad reviews for patterns
posts.x:
One bad review is a bad day. The same complaint three times is a problem you can fix.

Read your reviews once a month and look for repeats: late arrivals, surprise prices, no callback.

Fix the pattern, and the reviews follow.
posts.long:
One bad review is a bad day. The same complaint showing up three times is a problem you can actually fix.

Once a month, read through your reviews and your competitors' reviews. Look for things that repeat:
- "They showed up late"
- "The price was higher than the quote"
- "Nobody called me back"

Those aren't marketing problems. They're process problems, and they're usually fixable with a text, a policy or a quick talk with the team.

Fix the pattern and the reviews take care of themselves.

posts.headline: Your Google hours should match your phones
posts.x:
If Google says you're open until 6 but nobody answers after 4:30, homeowners notice.

Make your listed hours match when a real person picks up.

And update them for holidays before the holidays, not after.
posts.long:
If your Google profile says you're open until 6 but the phones go to voicemail at 4:30, homeowners notice, and some of them say so in a review.

Make your listed hours match when a real person answers.

While you're in there, set your holiday hours ahead of time for Christmas, New Year's and any days you close. Google lets you add special hours early, so people searching on the holiday see the truth.

It's a five-minute fix that saves a lot of frustrated calls.

posts.headline: Make booking one tap
posts.x:
If someone has to hunt for how to book, they leave.

One big button, on every page of your site: "Book a visit" or "Call now." Same on your Google profile.

Every extra step loses people.
posts.long:
If someone has to hunt for how to book you, a lot of them won't.

Check your website on your phone, the way homeowners see it:
- Is there one clear button at the top? "Call now" or "Book a visit."
- Does tapping your phone number actually dial it?
- Is the booking form short? Name, phone, what's wrong. That's enough to start.

Every extra field and every extra click loses people. Make it so easy that someone with a flooded basement can do it with one hand.

posts.headline: Use their name and the job in every follow-up
posts.x:
"Following up on your quote" sounds like a robot.

"Hi Karen, checking in on the water heater we looked at Tuesday" sounds like a person who remembers.

Name plus job. Every time.
posts.long:
"Just following up on your recent quote" sounds like it came from a machine.

"Hi Karen, checking in about the water heater we looked at on Tuesday. Any questions I can answer?" sounds like a real person who remembers you.

Every follow-up text or email should have:
- Their first name
- The specific job
- One easy question

It takes seconds longer and gets far more replies. People answer people.

posts.headline: Add value instead of cutting the price
posts.x:
When someone pushes on price, your first move doesn't have to be a discount.

Offer something that costs you little but means a lot to them: a longer labor warranty, a free check-up in six months, priority scheduling.

Keep your price. Raise the value.
posts.long:
When a homeowner pushes back on price, the quickest move is to knock some off. That trains people to haggle and eats your margin.

Try adding value instead. Things that cost you little but mean a lot to them:
- A longer labor warranty
- A free check-up in six months
- Priority scheduling if something goes wrong
- Hauling away the old unit

Now you've given them more reasons to say yes without lowering your price. Most people aren't looking for the cheapest company. They want to feel like they're getting a good deal.

posts.headline: Three questions to ask on every service call
posts.x:
Before the tech starts, three questions:
1. What's it doing?
2. When did it start?
3. When was it last serviced?

You learn the problem faster, and the homeowner feels heard.
posts.long:
Before the tech pulls a single tool out, three simple questions:
1. What's it doing, or not doing?
2. When did it start?
3. When was it last serviced?

They help the tech find the problem faster. They also tell you if this customer would be a good fit for a maintenance plan.

And they make the homeowner feel listened to. That matters more than most shops think. People forget a lot about a service call, but they remember whether the tech listened.

posts.headline: Remind members before the plan runs out
posts.x:
Maintenance plans don't renew themselves.

A month before the plan ends, send a short note: "Your plan is up for renewal next month. Want us to keep you on the schedule?"

Most people say yes when you ask early.
posts.long:
Maintenance plans are only steady income if people renew them, and most people won't remember to on their own.

About 30 days before a plan ends, send a short, friendly note:
"Hi Mark, your maintenance plan with us is up for renewal next month. Want us to keep you on the schedule? Just reply yes."

Easy to answer, no hard sell. Follow up once if you don't hear back.

Companies that ask early keep a lot more members than the ones that wait until it's already lapsed.

posts.headline: Shoe covers win reviews
posts.x:
Homeowners notice small things: shoe covers, a drop cloth, a clean truck, a tech who wipes up before leaving.

Nobody writes a review about the capacitor. They write about how you treated their house.
posts.long:
Homeowners rarely know if the repair was done the best way. What they do know is how you treated their house.

The small things show up in reviews again and again:
- Shoe covers on at the door
- A drop cloth under the work
- Cleaning up before leaving
- A clean truck and a clean uniform

Nobody writes a review about the capacitor. They write "he even put on shoe covers and cleaned up after himself."

Cheap habits. Big difference.

posts.headline: The one-minute walk-through
posts.x:
Before the tech leaves, a one-minute walk-through: here's what was wrong, here's what I did, here's what to watch for.

The homeowner understands what they paid for, and that's the perfect moment to ask for a review.
posts.long:
Before the tech packs up, take one minute to walk the homeowner through it:
- "Here's what was wrong."
- "Here's what I did."
- "Here's what to keep an eye on."

Show them the old part if you can. People feel better about the bill when they can see what they paid for.

That moment, when they're relieved and it's fixed, is also the best time to ask for a review. They're happy, you're standing right there, and the details are fresh.

posts.headline: Send freeze tips before the cold snap
posts.x:
When the forecast shows a hard freeze, text past customers a few tips: drip the faucets, open the sink cabinets, disconnect the hoses, know where your shutoff is.

It's genuinely helpful, and they'll remember who sent it.
posts.long:
When the forecast shows a hard freeze coming, send your past customers a short, helpful message:

"Hard freeze coming this weekend. A few quick tips:
- Let faucets on outside walls drip
- Open the cabinet doors under sinks
- Disconnect garden hoses
- Know where your main water shutoff is"

That's it. No sales pitch.

It might save someone a burst pipe. And if a pipe does burst, guess whose number they already have in their phone.

posts.headline: Look at last year's jobs by town
posts.x:
Before the new year starts, sort last year's jobs by town or zip code.

You'll probably find a few neighborhoods where you did a lot of work.

That's where to focus your mailers, yard signs and Google posts.
posts.long:
Before the new year gets busy, pull last year's jobs and sort them by town or zip code.

Most shops find something they didn't expect: a few neighborhoods where they did a lot of work, and some areas where they barely did any.

Use it:
- Put your Google posts and yard signs where you're already strong
- Ask yourself why the slow areas are slow. Too far? Wrong type of homes?
- Check that your best towns are named on your website

Your own job history is free market research.
